ai.definition: Quantum computing in materials science refers to the application of quantum computers to simulate and analyze the behavior of materials at the atomic or molecular scale.
ai.howItWorks: By leveraging qubits that can exist in multiple states simultaneously (superposition) and entanglement, quantum computers can model complex interactions within molecules more accurately than classical computers. This allows for the precise simulation of material properties and behaviors under various conditions.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional computational methods struggle with simulating large-scale molecular systems due to exponential growth in required computational resources. Quantum computing offers a way to overcome these limitations, enabling detailed simulations that were previously impractical or impossible.
ai.manufacturing: Current quantum computers are primarily built using superconducting circuits and trapped ions, though other technologies like topological qubits are under development.
ai.buildProcess: Involves cryogenic cooling, precise control of qubit states through microwave pulses, and error correction techniques to maintain coherence over longer periods.
ai.costDrivers: High cost associated with maintaining ultra-cold temperatures, complex hardware requirements, and the need for advanced algorithms and software.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected growth as quantum technologies mature and become more accessible.
ai.regulation: Lack of specific regulations; existing guidelines from organizations like NIST may apply.
ai.risks: Technical challenges in scaling up qubit counts, maintaining coherence, and developing robust error correction methods. Financial risks due to high initial investment costs.
ai.profitability: Potential for significant cost savings in R&D but currently limited by the technology's immaturity and high costs.
ai.futureDevelopment: Focus on improving qubit quality, increasing qubit count, and developing more efficient algorithms and software.

glossary.def: The basic unit of quantum information, analogous to a classical bit but capable of existing in multiple states simultaneously.
A principle of quantum mechanics where particles can exist in multiple states at once until measured.
A phenomenon in which the quantum state of one particle is dependent on the state of another, even when separated by large distances.

subsystems.name: Quantum processing unit
subsystems.role: the qubits that represent the electrons of the molecule or material.
parts: superconducting transmon chip, trapped-ion chain or neutral-atom array

subsystems.name: Encoding layer
subsystems.role: translates a chemistry problem into a form the qubits can hold.

subsystems.name: Error handling
subsystems.role: keeps noise from destroying the answer.
parts: error-mitigation schemes such as zero-noise extrapolation
error-correcting codes (surface code) and logical qubits

subsystems.name: Algorithm stack
subsystems.role: the procedure run on the hardware to find energies and properties.

subsystems.name: Classical co-processor
subsystems.role: optimises circuit parameters and stores results, in a tight loop with the quantum device.

subsystems.name: Validation and workflow
subsystems.role: checks the answer against trusted classical methods and feeds it into real design work.
parts: density functional theory, coupled cluster, DMRG or quantum Monte Carlo references

buildSteps.title: Pick a problem classical computers cannot solve
buildSteps.detail: Target strongly correlated systems — transition-metal catalysts, battery electrolytes, magnetic oxides — where density functional theory is unreliable.

buildSteps.title: Define the active space
buildSteps.detail: Choose which electrons and orbitals matter, and a basis set, to keep the problem small enough to encode.

buildSteps.title: Map the Hamiltonian to qubits
buildSteps.detail: Write the electronic Hamiltonian in second quantisation, then convert fermionic operators into qubit operators using a Jordan–Wigner or Bravyi–Kitaev mapping.

buildSteps.title: Estimate the resources needed
buildSteps.detail: Work out how many qubits, how deep a circuit, and how many measurements the problem demands; this usually shows present hardware is far too small and noisy.

buildSteps.title: Prepare and measure trial states
buildSteps.detail: On hardware today, run a variational eigensolver: prepare a parameterised state, measure its energy, and let a classical optimiser adjust the parameters.

buildSteps.title: Mitigate or correct errors
buildSteps.detail: Apply zero-noise extrapolation and similar techniques now; move to error-corrected logical qubits for the accuracy chemistry requires (roughly millihartree, or about 0.03 eV).

buildSteps.title: Extract observables
buildSteps.detail: Read out energies, forces, reaction barriers and spectra from the measured state rather than only the ground-state energy.

buildSteps.title: Validate against benchmarks
buildSteps.detail: Compare with coupled-cluster or experimental values; discard results that only look precise because of noise.

buildSteps.title: Embed in a design pipeline
buildSteps.detail: Feed validated numbers into classical molecular dynamics or screening workflows that propose new catalysts, electrolytes or superconductors.

prerequisites.why: chemistry needs far more accurate qubits than today's noisy devices provide; logical qubits are still at the demonstration stage.
methods exist and have run on small molecules, but resource estimates for useful problems remain out of reach.
ground-state energies of a few small molecules have been computed on quantum hardware, without outperforming classical methods.
density functional theory and coupled cluster are the baseline every quantum result must beat or complement.
cold atoms and Rydberg arrays can emulate model spin systems directly, offering materials insight before general-purpose quantum computers mature.
dilution refrigerators and microwave control are mature, but scaling to many thousands of qubits is not.

pathway.milestone: hybrid variational calculations of small molecules and analogue simulation of model magnets
pathway.unlocks: proof that the mapping, algorithms and hardware can work together at all.

pathway.milestone: early error-corrected machines with tens to hundreds of logical qubits
pathway.unlocks: accurate ground-state energies for problems just beyond classical reach.

pathway.milestone: quantum advantage on a recognised materials problem, validated against experiment
pathway.unlocks: industrial interest, funding and a reason to scale hardware further.

pathway.milestone: quantum chemistry as a routine step inside commercial materials-discovery pipelines
pathway.unlocks: faster design of catalysts, batteries and superconductors — the actual promise of the field.
